title: The Fake Amethyst Switch
markdown:
Mentor Vale entrusted Kian with a necklace that hummed, almost, with other people’s certainty. At its centre lay an amethyst so flawless, so radiant, that Lady Isolde — collector of the exquisite, rumoured to acquire the unattainable — declared it the finest specimen ever unearthed.

Beside Kian, Pip the otter offered a soft inquisitive churrup. Whiskers twitched. Pip’s snout nudged Kian’s palm. Kian turned the necklace over in the workshop light and felt it too: a faint unease in the gem’s dazzling core. Perfection on the surface was not always truth underneath. The science club’s gemstone exhibition was days away. Reputation, and the integrity of the display, rested on whether he could tell a mountain’s work from a vat’s.

He led Pip to their sanctuary — cluttered, kind, smelling faintly of ozone and tea gone cold. Wires. Beakers. A cork that had already escaped once and would again. From a velvet-lined case he took a microscope. He did not expect to see atoms with a school instrument. He expected to see how the stone had grown.

Magnified, the truth unfurled slowly, the way good news and bad news both do. Not a different crystal species. Still purple quartz. Still an ordered lattice, the same family of architecture that makes amethyst amethyst. But the growth did not look like a mountain’s slow argument with time. A faint seed-plate ghost, flat as a decision. Colour zoning too even, too obedient, like a story with no weather in it. A synthetic, grown to mimic allure with breathtaking accuracy.

Pip chirped and nudged toward a genuine amethyst Kian kept for comparison, a stone with a small scar of inclusion like a remembered cloud. Light moved through them differently at the edges. The natural held tiny interruptions, a little history trapped in the glass of it. The impostor was almost too clean. No magic hum under the lens. No different physics of soul. A story of origin, written in how the crystal had been allowed to grow.

Kian sat with that. Bittersweet. Isolde would not like being wrong. The stone was still beautiful. He could have loved it as lab-grown. Beauty was not the lie. The claim of unearthed was.

They went back the next evening and looked again, because once is a hunch and twice is a note. Pip kept the genuine stone from rolling. Kian sketched the seed line. Vale, passing, did not snatch the conclusion from him. She only said, “Bring both to the hall. Let the club see what you saw.”

Exhibition day. Earth’s treasures, catalogued by enthusiastic young scientists, a kaleidoscope of rocks that had nothing to prove except themselves. The air buzzed. Isolde stood in emerald velvet, ready to unveil. Kian did not stage a cork chase or a sleight of hand. He asked, politely, if the club might see how two purple stones could look alike and not share a history.

Portable spectroscope. Side by side, the necklace’s centre stone and his known natural. He spoke quietly. Lab-grown quartz can share a lattice with the mountain kind. What it often cannot hide is the seed, the too-even colour, the lack of the little accidents nature leaves. The fingerprint of a plate. The messy honesty of inclusions. Vale’s eyes were kind. A few students leaned in, then further in.

Isolde’s face tightened. She did not thunder. She left with a stammer, dignity cracked, not destroyed. The hall was quieter than victory usually is. Someone still admired the colour. That seemed fair.

“The value,” Vale said, not loudly, “is not only dazzle. Crystallography is the architecture — and also the growth. Lab and mountain can share a lattice. Origin still leaves a mark, if you look for it.”

Kian and Pip exchanged a glance. The world was full of hidden orders. Science asked for precision, and a little mercy. He wondered what else gleamed honestly, and what else only pretended to have come from the ground.
characters: Kian (a puzzle-loving physicist), Pip (an otter), Vale (a mentor)
